[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Your first program[/color][/b][/font_size]

Welcome, new shell-mate! I'm Pinch. Let's get you writing real Rust right away.

A program is just a list of instructions the computer follows, top to bottom. Rust programs always start in one special spot, a function called [code][color=#ffd36e]main[/color][/code].

[b][color=#e59cff]fn[/color][/b]  —  [i]short for "function", a named bundle of instructions. You make one with the word [code][color=#ffd36e]fn[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]main[/color][/b]  —  [i]the function Rust runs first when your program starts.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]println![/color][/b]  —  [i]prints a line of text on the screen, then moves to the next line.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]string[/color][/b]  —  [i]text wrapped in double quotes, like [code][color=#ffd36e]"Hello"[/color][/code].[/i]

See how [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code] ends with a [code][color=#ffd36e]![/color][/code]? That means it is a [b]macro[/b], a special helper that Rust expands into more code for you. For now just remember to type the [code][color=#ffd36e]![/color][/code].

Here is a whole program:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {                             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Hi from the sea floor!"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Second line."[/color]);           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                       [/bgcolor][/code]

A few things to notice:

   •  The instructions live between the curly braces [code][color=#ffd36e]{[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]}[/color][/code].

   •  Each instruction ends with a semicolon [code][color=#ffd36e];[/color][/code]. It works like a full stop in a sentence.

   •  Text must be in double quotes, and what you type is exactly what gets printed.

Your turn: the starter code is close but says slightly the wrong things. Fix the text so it prints the right lines.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: the compiler is picky about every comma and quote, and that is a good thing. It catches typos before they bite you![/i][/color]

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Variables[/color][/b][/font_size]

A variable is a labelled bucket that holds a value, so you can use it again later.

[b][color=#e59cff]let[/color][/b]  —  [i]creates a new variable. [code][color=#ffd36e]let lives = 3;[/color][/code] puts the value 3 in a bucket named [code][color=#ffd36e]lives[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]mut[/color][/b]  —  [i]short for "mutable". It allows a variable's value to change later.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]shadowing[/color][/b]  —  [i]making a brand new variable with the same name using [code][color=#ffd36e]let[/color][/code] again. The new one hides the old one.[/i]

Here is the surprising part: in Rust, variables [b]cannot change by default[/b].

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] coins = [color=#f78c6c]5[/color];                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Coins: {}"[/color], coins); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] steps = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color];            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     steps = steps + [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Steps: {}"[/color], steps); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                 [/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]coins[/color][/code] is locked. If you wrote [code][color=#ffd36e]coins = 6;[/color][/code] the compiler would refuse (error E0384). [code][color=#ffd36e]steps[/color][/code] has [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code], so changing it is fine.

The [code][color=#ffd36e]{}[/color][/code] inside [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code] is a placeholder. Rust swaps it for the value of the variable listed after the text.

So [code][color=#ffd36e]println!("Steps: {}", steps);[/color][/code] prints [code][color=#ffd36e]Steps: 1[/color][/code]. Use one [code][color=#ffd36e]{}[/color][/code] for each value you list.

Shadowing looks like this:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] size = [color=#f78c6c]3[/color];                                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] size = size + [color=#f78c6c]1[/color]; [color=#7f8ca3]// a new variable, now 4[/color] [/bgcolor][/code]

Your turn: the starter tries to change a locked variable, so it won't compile. Read the error message, then unlock the variable.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: locked-by-default is a safety feature. When you see [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code], you know that value is going to change somewhere.[/i][/color]

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Types[/color][/b][/font_size]

Every value in Rust has a [b]type[/b], which says what kind of thing it is. Numbers, text, and yes/no answers are all different kinds.

[b][color=#e59cff]i32[/color][/b]  —  [i]a whole number that can be negative. Like [code][color=#ffd36e]-5[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]0[/color][/code], or [code][color=#ffd36e]42[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]u32[/color][/b]  —  [i]a whole number that is never negative (the "u" is for "unsigned").[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]f64[/color][/b]  —  [i]a number with a decimal point, like [code][color=#ffd36e]2.5[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]bool[/color][/b]  —  [i]either [code][color=#ffd36e]true[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]false[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]char[/color][/b]  —  [i]a single character in single quotes, like [code][color=#ffd36e]'A'[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]&str[/color][/b]  —  [i]a piece of text in double quotes, like [code][color=#ffd36e]"Pinch"[/color][/code].[/i]

You can tell Rust the type yourself with a [b]type annotation[/b]: a colon and the type after the name.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] crabs: i32 = [color=#f78c6c]5[/color];       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] speed: f64 = [color=#f78c6c]2.5[/color];     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] happy: bool = [color=#c792ea]true[/color];   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] grade: char = [color=#c3e88d]'A'[/color];    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] name: &str = [color=#c3e88d]"Pinch"[/color]; [/bgcolor][/code]

One sneaky detail: whole numbers and decimals divide differently.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] a = [color=#f78c6c]7[/color] / [color=#f78c6c]2[/color];     [color=#7f8ca3]// 3   (whole numbers drop the remainder)[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] b = [color=#f78c6c]7.0[/color] / [color=#f78c6c]2.0[/color]; [color=#7f8ca3]// 3.5 (decimals keep it)[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]5[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]5.0[/color][/code] are different types. Rust won't mix them up for you, so add the [code][color=#ffd36e].0[/color][/code] when you want a decimal.[/i][/color]

In the starter, each little function should hand back a value of the right type. The part after [code][color=#ffd36e]->[/color][/code] is the type it returns.

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Functions[/color][/b][/font_size]

You've already used [code][color=#ffd36e]main[/color][/code]. Now let's build our own functions, little machines that take something in and give something back.

[b][color=#e59cff]parameter[/color][/b]  —  [i]a named input to a function, written with its type: [code][color=#ffd36e]n: i32[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]return type[/color][/b]  —  [i]the type of the value a function hands back, written after [code][color=#ffd36e]->[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]expression[/color][/b]  —  [i]a piece of code that produces a value, like [code][color=#ffd36e]n * 2[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]statement[/color][/b]  —  [i]an instruction that does something but produces no value, like a line ending in [code][color=#ffd36e];[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]format![/color][/b]  —  [i]like [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code], but instead of printing it gives you the text as a [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code].[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] double(n: i32) -> i32 {       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     n * [color=#f78c6c]2[/color]                        [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {                      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] result = double([color=#f78c6c]4[/color]);      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], result); [color=#7f8ca3]// 8[/color] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                [/bgcolor][/code]

Look closely at [code][color=#ffd36e]n * 2[/color][/code]. It has [b]no semicolon[/b]. The last expression in a function is its return value. Add a [code][color=#ffd36e];[/color][/code] and it turns into a statement that produces nothing, and the compiler will complain.

To call a function, write its name and put the inputs in parentheses: [code][color=#ffd36e]double(4)[/color][/code].

Here is [code][color=#ffd36e]format![/color][/code] in action:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] msg = [color=#82aaff]format[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Ahoy, {}!"[/color], [color=#c3e88d]"sailor"[/color]); [color=#7f8ca3]// "Ahoy, sailor!"[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

It builds text just like [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code] does, but hands it back to you instead of printing it.

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Tide Decisions[/color][/b][/font_size]

So far your programs run top to bottom, no questions asked. Time to teach them to *choose*.

[b][color=#e59cff]If[/color][/b]  —  [i]runs a block of code only when a condition is true. The condition must be a [code][color=#ffd36e]bool[/color][/code] ([code][color=#ffd36e]true[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]false[/color][/code]).[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]else[/color][/b]  —  [i]the block that runs when the [code][color=#ffd36e]if[/color][/code] condition was false.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]else if[/color][/b]  —  [i]another condition to try when the earlier ones were false.[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] water = [color=#f78c6c]4[/color];             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]if[/color] water < [color=#f78c6c]2[/color] {             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Low tide"[/color]);  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] } [color=#c792ea]else[/color] [color=#c792ea]if[/color] water < [color=#f78c6c]6[/color] {      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Mid tide"[/color]);  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] } [color=#c792ea]else[/color] {                   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"High tide"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                          [/bgcolor][/code]

Rust checks the conditions from the top and runs the [b]first[/b] block that matches. No parentheses are needed around the condition.

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff]Asking questions[/color][/b][/font_size]

[b][color=#e59cff]Comparison operators[/color][/b]  —  [i][code][color=#ffd36e]==[/color][/code] equal, [code][color=#ffd36e]!=[/color][/code] not equal, [code][color=#ffd36e]<[/color][/code] less, [code][color=#ffd36e]>[/color][/code] greater, [code][color=#ffd36e]<=[/color][/code] less or equal, [code][color=#ffd36e]>=[/color][/code] greater or equal. Each gives back a [code][color=#ffd36e]bool[/color][/code].[/i]

You can combine yes/no answers:

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]a && b[/color][/code] means both must be true ("and")

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]a || b[/color][/code] means at least one is true ("or")

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]!a[/color][/code] flips true to false and back ("not")

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff][code][color=#ffd36e]if[/color][/code] hands back a value[/color][/b][/font_size]

In Rust, [code][color=#ffd36e]if[/color][/code] is an [b]expression[/b], so it can produce a value:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] mood = [color=#c792ea]if[/color] water > [color=#f78c6c]5[/color] { [color=#c3e88d]"splashy"[/color] } [color=#c792ea]else[/color] { [color=#c3e88d]"calm"[/color] };[/bgcolor][/code]

Every branch must give the same type, and there is no semicolon after the value inside the braces. This is also how a function can end with an [code][color=#ffd36e]if[/color][/code] and return its result.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: the [code][color=#ffd36e]'static[/color][/code] in [code][color=#ffd36e]&'static str[/color][/code] just means the text is baked into the program. Treat it as "a piece of text" for now![/i][/color]

For [code][color=#ffd36e]is_beach_day[/color][/code], join three yes/no answers with [code][color=#ffd36e]&&[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]height >= 2 && height <= 6 && !raining[/color][/code].

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Round and Round[/color][/b][/font_size]

Crabs scuttle back and forth all day. Programs need to repeat things too, and Rust gives you three ways.

[b][color=#e59cff]loop[/color][/b]  —  [i]repeats forever, until you stop it with [code][color=#ffd36e]break[/color][/code].[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]break[/color][/b]  —  [i]jumps out of the nearest loop.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]while[/color][/b]  —  [i]repeats as long as its condition is true.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]for[/color][/b]  —  [i]walks through a range (or other collection), one item at a time.[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] steps = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color];  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]loop[/color] {              [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     steps += [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]if[/color] steps == [color=#f78c6c]3[/color] { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]break[/color];      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }               [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                   [/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]steps += 1[/color][/code] is shorthand for [code][color=#ffd36e]steps = steps + 1[/color][/code]. The variable has to be [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code] because it changes.

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff]while and for[/color][/b][/font_size]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] n = [color=#f78c6c]10[/color];             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]while[/color] n > [color=#f78c6c]7[/color] {               [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{n}"[/color]);        [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     n -= [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] i [color=#c792ea]in[/color] [color=#f78c6c]1[/color]..=[color=#f78c6c]3[/color] {            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"pinch #{i}"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                           [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]Range[/color][/b]  —  [i][code][color=#ffd36e]1..=3[/color][/code] means 1, 2, 3 (both ends included). [code][color=#ffd36e]1..3[/color][/code] stops *before* 3, so it gives only 1 and 2.[/i]

Use [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code] when you know what to walk through, [code][color=#ffd36e]while[/color][/code] when you repeat until something changes.

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff]Collecting a total[/color][/b][/font_size]

A very common pattern is an [b]accumulator[/b]: a [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code] variable that starts at 0 and grows each time around.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] total = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color]; [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] i [color=#c792ea]in[/color] [color=#f78c6c]1[/color]..=[color=#f78c6c]4[/color] {   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     total += i;    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// total is now 10[/color] [/bgcolor][/code]

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: if your program seems frozen, you may have a [code][color=#ffd36e]loop[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]while[/color][/code] that never ends. Press Ctrl+C and check your [code][color=#ffd36e]break[/color][/code] or your condition![/i][/color]
lessons.goal: Write [code][color=#ffd36e]sum_to[/color][/code] (add 1 through n with a [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code] loop), [code][color=#ffd36e]doublings[/color][/code] (count how many times 1 must double with a [code][color=#ffd36e]while[/color][/code] loop to pass a limit), and make [code][color=#ffd36e]main[/color][/code] print the crab count for 1 to 15 exactly as in the comments.
hints: For [code][color=#ffd36e]sum_to[/color][/code]: make [code][color=#ffd36e]let mut total = 0;[/color][/code], loop with [code][color=#ffd36e]for i in 1..=n[/color][/code], do [code][color=#ffd36e]total += i;[/color][/code], and end the function with just [code][color=#ffd36e]total[/color][/code].

For [code][color=#ffd36e]doublings[/color][/code], keep two mut variables, [code][color=#ffd36e]value[/color][/code] (starts at 1) and [code][color=#ffd36e]count[/color][/code] (starts at 0). [font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Who Owns the Shell?[/color][/b][/font_size]

A hermit crab owns exactly one shell. If it hands the shell to a friend, the friend owns it now, and the first crab can't live there anymore. Rust treats data the same way. This is the idea that makes Rust special.

[b][color=#e59cff]Ownership[/color][/b]  —  [i]every value has exactly one owner (a variable). When the owner goes away, the value is cleaned up automatically.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]Move[/color][/b]  —  [i]giving a value to another variable or a function transfers ownership. The old variable can no longer be used.[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] a = [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"shell"[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] b = a;              [color=#7f8ca3]// the String MOVES from a to b[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], a);      [color=#7f8ca3]// error[lb]E0382[rb]: borrow of moved value: `a`[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

That error code, [b]E0382[/b], means "you used something after it moved". Remember it, you'll meet it again!

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff]Numbers just get copied[/color][/b][/font_size]

[b][color=#e59cff]Copy[/color][/b]  —  [i]simple, small types like [code][color=#ffd36e]i32[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]f64[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]bool[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]char[/color][/code] are copied instead of moved, so both variables stay usable.[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] x = [color=#f78c6c]5[/color];                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] y = x;                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{x} {y}"[/color]);    [color=#7f8ca3]// fine![/color] [/bgcolor][/code]

A [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code] owns text on the heap, so copying it silently would be costly. Rust moves it instead.

[font_size=30][b][color=#7fd1ff]Two ways out[/color][/b][/font_size]

[b][color=#e59cff]Clone[/color][/b]  —  [i][code][color=#ffd36e].clone()[/color][/code] makes a full, separate copy. Both copies have an owner. It works, but copying costs time and memory.[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]Borrow[/color][/b]  —  [i][code][color=#ffd36e]&name[/color][/code] lets someone *look* at a value without owning it. The owner keeps the shell.[/i]

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] shell_size(s: &[color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]) -> usize {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     s.len()[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] shell = [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"spiral"[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] n = shell_size(&shell);   [color=#7f8ca3]// borrow with &[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{shell} {n}"[/color]);      [color=#7f8ca3]// shell still works[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

The [code][color=#ffd36e]&String[/color][/code] in the parameter means "I only want to borrow a String". The [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code] at the call site hands over the loan.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: when a function only needs to look, borrow with [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code]. Reach for [code][color=#ffd36e].clone()[/color][/code] only when you truly need a second copy.[/i][/color]

Then lend the value at the call: [code][color=#ffd36e]name_length(&name)[/color][/code]. The [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code] goes in both places.

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Make your own type[/color][/b][/font_size]

So far you have used types Rust gave you, like [code][color=#ffd36e]i32[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code]. Now you get to invent your own!

A [b]struct[/b] bundles several values into one thing, and each value gets a name.

[b][color=#e59cff]struct[/color][/b]  —  [i]a custom type made of named pieces of data[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]field[/color][/b]  —  [i]one named piece inside a struct[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]impl[/color][/b]  —  [i]a block where you attach functions to a type[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]method[/color][/b]  —  [i]a function that works on one particular value; you call it with a dot[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]associated function[/color][/b]  —  [i]a function in an [code][color=#ffd36e]impl[/color][/code] block that has no [code][color=#ffd36e]self[/color][/code]; you call it with [code][color=#ffd36e]::[/color][/code][/i]

Here is a tiny example about a fish:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]struct[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     name: [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color],[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     length: u32,[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]impl[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#7f8ca3]// associated function: builds a new Fish[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] new(name: &str) -> [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color] { name: name.to_string(), length: [color=#f78c6c]1[/color] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#7f8ca3]// method: only reads (&self)[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] is_big(&[color=#c792ea]self[/color]) -> bool {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]self[/color].length > [color=#f78c6c]30[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#7f8ca3]// method: changes the fish (&mut self)[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] grow(&[color=#c792ea]mut[/color] [color=#c792ea]self[/color], cm: u32) {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]self[/color].length += cm;[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] f = [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color]::new([color=#c3e88d]"Bubbles"[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     f.grow([color=#f78c6c]40[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{} is {} cm"[/color], f.name, f.length);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

Notice a few things:

   •  You read a field with a dot: [code][color=#ffd36e]f.length[/color][/code].

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]&self[/color][/code] means "borrow me to look". [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut self[/color][/code] means "borrow me to change", so the variable must be [code][color=#ffd36e]let mut[/color][/code].

   •  Inside a method, [code][color=#ffd36e]self[/color][/code] is the value itself, so you write [code][color=#ffd36e]self.length[/color][/code].

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]Fish::new(...)[/color][/code] uses [code][color=#ffd36e]::[/color][/code] because [code][color=#ffd36e]new[/color][/code] has no [code][color=#ffd36e]self[/color][/code].

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]new[/color][/code] is not a special keyword. It is just a popular name for "build me one of these". Nice and tidy![/i][/color]
lessons.goal: Fill in the three todo!() bodies in the Crab impl: new (name given, 0 shells), collect (adds n shells), and is_rich (true when the crab has 10 or more shells).
hints: Start with [code][color=#ffd36e]new[/color][/code]. You need to return a [code][color=#ffd36e]Crab { ... }[/color][/code] and give a value to both fields, [code][color=#ffd36e]name[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[/color][/code].

For the name field, a [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code] must become a [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code]: write [code][color=#ffd36e]name: name.to_string()[/color][/code]. Start [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[/color][/code] at [code][color=#ffd36e]0[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]collect[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]self.shells += n;[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]is_rich[/color][/code] is just the comparison [code][color=#ffd36e]self.shells >= 10[/color][/code] with no semicolon, so it is returned.

quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e]new[/color][/code] has no [code][color=#ffd36e]self[/color][/code], so it is an associated function and you call it with [code][color=#ffd36e]::[/color][/code] on the type name.

choices: No: f must be declared `let mut f`
No: Fish::new returns the wrong type
quizzes.explain: A [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut self[/color][/code] method changes the value, so the variable has to be [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code]. Rust reports E0596.
quizzes.question:
Does this compile? ([code][color=#ffd36e]grow[/color][/code] takes [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut self[/color][/code])

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] f = [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color]::new([color=#c3e88d]"Bubbles"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] f.grow([color=#f78c6c]5[/color]);                    [/bgcolor][/code]

quizzes.explain: The length starts at 1, then 1 + 20 + 15 = 36. That is more than 30, so is_big gives true.
quizzes.question:
What does this print?

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] f = [color=#ffcb6b]Fish[/color]::new([color=#c3e88d]"Bubbles"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] f.grow([color=#f78c6c]20[/color]);                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] f.grow([color=#f78c6c]15[/color]);                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], f.is_big());       [/bgcolor][/code]

lessons.success: Shell-ebration time! You made your own type: a struct holds named fields, and an impl block gives it an associated function (new) plus methods that read (&self) or change (&mut self) it.

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]One thing, several shapes[/color][/b][/font_size]

Sometimes a value can be one of a few different kinds. A traffic light is red, yellow, or green, never two at once. Rust models this with an [b]enum[/b].

[b][color=#e59cff]enum[/color][/b]  —  [i]a type whose value is exactly one of several named options[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]variant[/color][/b]  —  [i]one of the options inside an enum[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]match[/color][/b]  —  [i]checks a value against patterns, one arm at a time, and runs the first arm that fits[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]arm[/color][/b]  —  [i]one [code][color=#ffd36e]pattern => result[/color][/code] line inside a match[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]_[/color][/b]  —  [i]a catch-all pattern that matches anything not listed above it[/i]

Variants can carry data too:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]enum[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Seaweed[/color],[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Shrimp[/color](u32),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Plankton[/color] { scoops: u32 },[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] describe(s: &[color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]match[/color] s {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Seaweed[/color] => [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"just seaweed"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Shrimp[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]format[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{} shrimp"[/color], n),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Plankton[/color] { scoops } => [color=#82aaff]format[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{} scoops of plankton"[/color], scoops),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

You name a variant with [code][color=#ffd36e]::[/color][/code], like [code][color=#ffd36e]Snack::Shrimp(3)[/color][/code]. Inside a match arm you can pull the carried data out into a name, like [code][color=#ffd36e]n[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]scoops[/color][/code].

Here is the clever bit: [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] must cover [b]every[/b] possible variant. If you forget one, the compiler refuses with error [b]E0004[/b] ("non-exhaustive patterns"). That is a safety net, not a scolding. It means you can never forget a case.

Too many variants to list? End with [code][color=#ffd36e]_[/color][/code]:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]match[/color] s {                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Seaweed[/color] => [color=#f78c6c]1[/color], [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     _ => [color=#f78c6c]0[/color],              [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                        [/bgcolor][/code]

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: put [code][color=#ffd36e]_[/color][/code] last, because arms are checked from top to bottom. If it came first, it would grab everything![/i][/color]
lessons.goal: Finish [code][color=#ffd36e]advice[/color][/code] so it uses [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] on the Weather: Sunny gives "Wear sunglasses", Rainy(mm) with 10 or more mm gives "Stay in your shell", any lighter Rainy gives "Bring a seaweed umbrella", and Storm gives "Hide under a rock" (exact text).
hints: Start with [code][color=#ffd36e]match w {[/color][/code] and write one arm for each variant, like [code][color=#ffd36e]Weather::Sunny => ...,[/color][/code].

To grab the number inside Rainy, write [code][color=#ffd36e]Weather::Rainy(mm) => ...[/color][/code]. Because [code][color=#ffd36e]w[/color][/code] is a reference, [code][color=#ffd36e]mm[/color][/code] is a [code][color=#ffd36e]&u32[/color][/code], so compare with [code][color=#ffd36e]*mm >= 10[/color][/code]. For Storm, [code][color=#ffd36e]Weather::Storm { .. }[/color][/code] means "I do not need the wind".
An arm can hold a block: [code][color=#ffd36e]Weather::Rainy(mm) => { if *mm >= 10 { String::from("Stay in your shell") } else { String::from("Bring a seaweed umbrella") } }[/color][/code].

quizzes.explain: The Shrimp arm fits, and [code][color=#ffd36e]n[/color][/code] is the 3 it carries. The arm prints n + 1, which is 4.
quizzes.question:
What does this print?

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]enum[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Seaweed[/color],[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Shrimp[/color](u32),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] s = [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Shrimp[/color]([color=#f78c6c]3[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]match[/color] s {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Seaweed[/color] => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"weed"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Snack[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Shrimp[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{} shrimp"[/color], n + [color=#f78c6c]1[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

choices: No: E0004, Yellow is not covered
No: Red needs to carry data
Yes, s becomes an empty string
quizzes.explain: A match must cover every variant. Add a [code][color=#ffd36e]Light::Yellow[/color][/code] arm or finish with [code][color=#ffd36e]_[/color][/code].
quizzes.question:
Does this compile?

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]enum[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Light[/color] { [color=#ffcb6b]Red[/color], [color=#ffcb6b]Yellow[/color], [color=#ffcb6b]Green[/color] } [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] l = [color=#ffcb6b]Light[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Red[/color];               [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] s = [color=#c792ea]match[/color] l {                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Light[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Red[/color] => [color=#c3e88d]"stop"[/color],         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Light[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Green[/color] => [color=#c3e88d]"go"[/color],         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] };                                [/bgcolor][/code]

quizzes.explain: Arms are checked top to bottom and [code][color=#ffd36e]_[/color][/code] matches anything, so the first arm wins. The [code][color=#ffd36e]5[/color][/code] arm can never run, and the compiler warns about an unreachable pattern.
quizzes.question:
What does this print? (It compiles, with a warning.)

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] n = [color=#f78c6c]5[/color];           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] word = [color=#c792ea]match[/color] n { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     _ => [color=#c3e88d]"other"[/color],    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#f78c6c]5[/color] => [color=#c3e88d]"five"[/color],     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] };                   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{word}"[/color]);  [/bgcolor][/code]

lessons.success: Match made in the deep! An enum says "one of these shapes", and match makes the compiler check that you handled every shape. No forgotten cases, ever.

taps.prompt: Finish [code][color=#ffd36e]advice[/color][/code] so it uses [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] on the Weather: Sunny gives "Wear sunglasses", Rainy(mm) with 10 or more mm gives "Stay in your shell", any lighter Rainy gives "Bring a seaweed umbrella", and Storm gives "Hide under a rock" (exact text).

lessons.title: Weather or Not

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]When things might go wrong[/color][/b][/font_size]

Looking for a shell on the beach? Maybe you find one, maybe you don't. Many languages use a special "null" value for "nothing here", and it causes crashes. Rust has no null. Instead it has two enums that make you deal with the problem up front.

[b][color=#e59cff]Option[/color][/b]  —  [i]an enum meaning "maybe a value": either [code][color=#ffd36e]Some(value)[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]Result[/color][/b]  —  [i]an enum meaning "worked or failed": either [code][color=#ffd36e]Ok(value)[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]Err(error)[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]if let[/color][/b]  —  [i]a short match that only cares about one pattern[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]?[/color][/b]  —  [i]inside a function that returns Result, passes an [code][color=#ffd36e]Err[/color][/code] straight back to the caller[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]unwrap[/color][/b]  —  [i]grabs the value inside, but crashes your whole program on [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]Err[/color][/code][/i]

Here they are in action:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] first_even(nums: &[lb]i32[rb]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]Option[/color]<i32> {   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]for[/color] &n [color=#c792ea]in[/color] nums {                           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]if[/color] n % [color=#f78c6c]2[/color] == [color=#f78c6c]0[/color] {                        [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]             [color=#c792ea]return[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](n);                    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         }                                      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]None[/color]                                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                              [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {                                    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]match[/color] first_even(&[lb][color=#f78c6c]3[/color], [color=#f78c6c]5[/color], [color=#f78c6c]8[/color][rb]) {             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"found {}"[/color], n),    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]None[/color] => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"no even numbers"[/color]),   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]if[/color] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](n) = first_even(&[lb][color=#f78c6c]1[/color], [color=#f78c6c]3[/color][rb]) {     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"this will not print {}"[/color], n); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]match[/color] [color=#c3e88d]"42"[/color].parse::<u32>() {                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Ok[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"number: {}"[/color], n),    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#ffcb6b]Err[/color](_) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"not a number"[/color]),    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                              [/bgcolor][/code]

The type [code][color=#ffd36e]&[lb]i32[rb][/color][/code] is a [b]slice[/b]: a borrowed view of a list of values. [code][color=#ffd36e]&[lb]&str[rb][/color][/code] is a slice of text pieces.

You can use [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] on both types, just like an enum, because they are enums. The compiler makes you handle [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]Err[/color][/code], so a missing value can't sneak up on you.

Calling [code][color=#ffd36e].unwrap()[/color][/code] skips that safety: it panics (crashes) when there is no value. Fine for quick experiments, risky for real programs.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: when a function can fail, return a Result and let the caller decide what to do. Much kinder than a crash![/i][/color]
lessons.goal: Write find_shell (return Some(index) of the first matching name in the slice, or None) and parse_depth (turn text into a u32 as Ok, or return Err with a friendly message that includes the text), without using unwrap().
hints: For find_shell, loop over positions with [code][color=#ffd36e]for i in 0..shells.len()[/color][/code] and compare [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[lb]i[rb] == name[/color][/code]. When they match, [code][color=#ffd36e]return Some(i);[/color][/code].
If the loop finishes without finding anything, the last line of find_shell should be [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code] (no semicolon, no quotes).

For parse_depth, [code][color=#ffd36e]match text.parse::<u32>() { Ok(d) => Ok(d), Err(_) => Err(format!("'{}' is not a depth", text)) }[/color][/code]. The [code][color=#ffd36e]Ok[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]Err[/color][/code] on the left are what parse gives you; the ones on the right are what you return.

quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e]unwrap()[/color][/code] panics when there is no value. [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]if let[/color][/code] let you handle it, and [code][color=#ffd36e]?[/color][/code] passes an Err back to the caller.
quizzes.question: Which of these crashes your program when the value is [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]Err[/color][/code]?

quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e]get[/color][/code] returns an Option instead of crashing. Index 5 is past the end, so you get None.
quizzes.question:
What does this print?

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] v = [color=#82aaff]vec[/color]![lb][color=#f78c6c]10[/color], [color=#f78c6c]20[/color], [color=#f78c6c]30[/color][rb];           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]match[/color] v.get([color=#f78c6c]5[/color]) {                    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](x) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"got {x}"[/color]), [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]None[/color] => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"nothing"[/color]),    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                   [/bgcolor][/code]

choices: No: `?` needs a function that returns Result (or Option)
No: parse is not a method on &str
Yes, but it panics on bad text

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Borrowzilla rises from the tide pool![/color][/b][/font_size]

A giant monster guards the tide pool, and the only way past is to finish its [b]inventory[/b] of sea creatures. Every passing test knocks one HP off the boss.

You already know every tool you need:

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]struct[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]enum[/color][/code] hold the data (already defined for you)

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] picks an answer based on the enum

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]Option[/color][/code] says "maybe there is a value"

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code] loops repeat work

   •  [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut[/color][/code] borrow instead of taking ownership

Read the comments in the starter, then fill in each [code][color=#ffd36e]todo!()[/color][/code].

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: if a test fails, read its message. It tells you exactly what the boss expected. Beat him one function at a time![/i][/color]

hints: Take the functions top to bottom. [code][color=#ffd36e]points[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]kind_from_letter[/color][/code] are both [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code]. The second one needs a final [code][color=#ffd36e]_ => None[/color][/code] arm for every other letter.

[code][color=#ffd36e]kind_from_letter[/color][/code] returns [code][color=#ffd36e]Some(Kind::Crab)[/color][/code] for 'c' and so on. [code][color=#ffd36e]pile_score[/color][/code] needs [code][color=#ffd36e]let mut total = 0;[/color][/code], then [code][color=#ffd36e]for _ in 0..count { total += points(kind); }[/color][/code], then [code][color=#ffd36e]total[/color][/code] on its own line at the end.

[code][color=#ffd36e]grow[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]creature.size += 1;[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]label[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]format!("{} (size {})", creature.name, creature.size)[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]rename[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]creature.name = new_name.to_string();[/color][/code] because a [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code] must become an owned [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code].

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]One bucket, many shells[/color][/b][/font_size]

Until now each variable held one thing. What if you find 50 shells on the beach? You need a bucket!

A [b]Vec[/b] is a growable list that holds many values of the same type.

[b][color=#e59cff]Vec[/color][/b]  —  [i]a growable list of values that all have the same type, written [code][color=#ffd36e]Vec<i32>[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]vec![/color][/b]  —  [i]a macro that builds a Vec from values you list[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]push[/color][/b]  —  [i]a method that adds one item to the end of a Vec[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]index[/color][/b]  —  [i]the position of an item, counting from 0[/i]

Here is a bucket in action:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] shells = [color=#82aaff]vec[/color]![lb][color=#f78c6c]3[/color], [color=#f78c6c]8[/color], [color=#f78c6c]5[/color][rb];      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] shells.push([color=#f78c6c]10[/color]);                     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], shells.len());   [color=#7f8ca3]// 4[/color] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], shells[lb][color=#f78c6c]0[/color][rb]);      [color=#7f8ca3]// 3[/color] [/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]vec![lb]...[rb][/color][/code] makes the list. [code][color=#ffd36e]push[/color][/code] needs [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code], because the bucket changes. [code][color=#ffd36e]len()[/color][/code] tells you how many items are inside.

You can also start empty with [code][color=#ffd36e]Vec::new()[/color][/code] and push as you go. Rust figures out the type from what you push in.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: indexes start at 0, so the first shell is [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[lb]0[rb][/color][/code] and the last of four is [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[lb]3[rb][/color][/code].[/i][/color]

[b]Danger zone![/b] What if you ask for [code][color=#ffd36e]shells[lb]99[rb][/color][/code] and there are only 4? The program [b]panics[/b] and crashes.

The safe way is [code][color=#ffd36e].get(99)[/color][/code]. It returns an [code][color=#ffd36e]Option[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]Some(&value)[/color][/code] if the spot exists, or [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code] if not.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]match[/color] shells.get([color=#f78c6c]99[/color]) {                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"found {n}"[/color]),  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]None[/color] => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"nothing there"[/color]), [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                      [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]Option[/color][/b]  —  [i]you met it before! [code][color=#ffd36e]get[/color][/code] uses it to say "maybe there is a value here"[/i]

Use [code][color=#ffd36e][lb][rb][/color][/code] when you are sure the spot exists. Use [code][color=#ffd36e].get()[/color][/code] when you are not.

To visit every item, use [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code]. Borrow the Vec with [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code] so you can use it again afterwards:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] sum = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color];   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] s [color=#c792ea]in[/color] &shells { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     sum += s;      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                  [/bgcolor][/code]

To [b]change[/b] each item, borrow mutably with [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut[/color][/code]. Then [code][color=#ffd36e]s[/color][/code] is a reference, and you write [code][color=#ffd36e]*s[/color][/code] to reach the value inside:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] s [color=#c792ea]in[/color] &[color=#c792ea]mut[/color] shells { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     *s += [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];           [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                      [/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]*s[/color][/code] means "the thing [code][color=#ffd36e]s[/color][/code] points at". Functions can take [code][color=#ffd36e]&Vec<i32>[/color][/code] to look at a list or [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut Vec<i32>[/color][/code] to change it.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: a plain [code][color=#ffd36e]for s in shells[/color][/code] would move the whole Vec away. Add [code][color=#ffd36e]&[/color][/code] to keep it![/i][/color]
lessons.goal: Implement total (sum of the Vec), first_or_zero (first item, or 0 if empty, using .get), double_all (double every item in place) and countdown (a Vec from n down to 1).
hints: [code][color=#ffd36e]total[/color][/code]: make [code][color=#ffd36e]let mut sum = 0;[/color][/code], then [code][color=#ffd36e]for n in v { sum += n; }[/color][/code] (v is already a borrow), and end the function with [code][color=#ffd36e]sum[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]first_or_zero[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]match v.get(0) { Some(n) => *n, None => 0 }[/color][/code]. The [code][color=#ffd36e]*[/color][/code] turns the reference [code][color=#ffd36e]&i32[/color][/code] into a plain [code][color=#ffd36e]i32[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]double_all[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]for n in v { *n *= 2; }[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]countdown[/color][/code]: start with [code][color=#ffd36e]let mut out = Vec::new();[/color][/code] then push [code][color=#ffd36e]n[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]n - 1[/color][/code], ... down to 1 using a [code][color=#ffd36e]while[/color][/code] loop, and return [code][color=#ffd36e]out[/color][/code].

quizzes.explain: After the push there are 3 items, so len is 3. Indexes start at 0, so v[lb]1[rb] is the second item: 20.
quizzes.question:
What does this print?

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] v = [color=#82aaff]vec[/color]![lb][color=#f78c6c]10[/color], [color=#f78c6c]20[/color][rb];         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] v.push([color=#f78c6c]30[/color]);                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{} {}"[/color], v.len(), v[lb][color=#f78c6c]1[/color][rb]); [/bgcolor][/code]

quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e].get()[/color][/code] never panics. Out of range gives [code][color=#ffd36e]None[/color][/code]. Only [code][color=#ffd36e]v[lb]5[rb][/color][/code] would crash the program.
quizzes.question: A Vec has 3 items. What does [code][color=#ffd36e]v.get(5)[/color][/code] give back?

quizzes.explain: You need [code][color=#ffd36e]&mut v[/color][/code] to be allowed to change items, and [code][color=#ffd36e]*n[/color][/code] to reach the value behind the reference.
quizzes.question: Which loop adds 1 to every number inside [code][color=#ffd36e]v[/color][/code]?

lessons.success: Bucket full! A Vec holds many values of one type. Use [lb][rb] when you're sure, .get() when you're not, [code][color=#ffd36e]for x in &v[/color][/code] to look and [code][color=#ffd36e]for x in &mut v[/color][/code] to change.

cards:
[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Two kinds of text[/color][/b][/font_size]

You have met both already, but let's make it stick.

[b][color=#e59cff]String[/color][/b]  —  [i]owned text that lives in a variable and can grow[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]&str[/color][/b]  —  [i]a borrowed view of text, like a literal [code][color=#ffd36e]"hello"[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]push_str[/color][/b]  —  [i]adds more text onto the end of a [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]format![/color][/b]  —  [i]builds a new [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code] from pieces, like [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code] without printing[/i]

Rule of thumb: [b]take [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code] as input, give back [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code] as output[/b]. A [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code] parameter accepts both literals and borrowed Strings.

Building text:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] s = [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"Ahoy"[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] s.push_str([color=#c3e88d]", crab"[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] s.push([color=#c3e88d]'!'[/color]);                       [color=#7f8ca3]// one char uses push[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] msg = [color=#82aaff]format[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{s} x{}"[/color], [color=#f78c6c]3[/color]);   [color=#7f8ca3]// "Ahoy, crab! x3"[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], msg.len());         [color=#7f8ca3]// 14[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]len()[/color][/code] counts [b]bytes[/b], which equals letters for plain English text.

A function that changes a String must borrow it mutably: [code][color=#ffd36e]fn add_bang(s: &mut String) { s.push('!'); }[/color][/code].

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]"abc" + "def"[/color][/code] does not work in Rust. Use [code][color=#ffd36e]format![/color][/code] to glue text together instead.[/i][/color]

Asking questions about text. These methods work on [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code]:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] t = [color=#c3e88d]"  big red crab  "[/color];[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] t.trim();                    [color=#7f8ca3]// "big red crab"[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] t.contains([color=#c3e88d]"red"[/color]);           [color=#7f8ca3]// true[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] t.to_uppercase();            [color=#7f8ca3]// "  BIG RED CRAB  " (a new String)[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] t.split_whitespace().count() [color=#7f8ca3]// 3 words[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]trim[/color][/b]  —  [i]removes spaces from both ends[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]split_whitespace[/color][/b]  —  [i]cuts text into words, ignoring extra spaces; use it in a [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code] loop or call [code][color=#ffd36e].count()[/color][/code][/i]

Letter by letter, use [code][color=#ffd36e].chars()[/color][/code] in a loop:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] e = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color];                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] ch [color=#c792ea]in[/color] [color=#c3e88d]"seashell"[/color].chars() { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]if[/color] ch == [color=#c3e88d]'e'[/color] {             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         e += [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];                [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                              [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// e is 2[/color]                      [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]chars[/color][/b]  —  [i]gives you each character one at a time[/i]

Single characters use single quotes ([code][color=#ffd36e]'e'[/color][/code]), text uses double quotes ([code][color=#ffd36e]"e"[/color][/code]).

Methods like [code][color=#ffd36e]to_uppercase()[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]trim()[/color][/code] don't change the original. They give you something new.

[code][color=#ffd36e]word_count[/color][/code] is one line: [code][color=#ffd36e]s.split_whitespace().count()[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]banner[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]format!("{} has {} shells", name.trim(), shells)[/color][/code]. quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e]trim()[/color][/code] removes the spaces at both ends, leaving "big red crab", which is 12 bytes long.

[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], t.trim().len()); [/bgcolor][/code]

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]A notebook with labels[/color][/b][/font_size]

A Vec finds things by position. A [b]HashMap[/b] finds things by [b]name[/b], like a notebook where each page has a label.

[b][color=#e59cff]HashMap[/color][/b]  —  [i]a collection of key and value pairs; look up a value by its key[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]key[/color][/b]  —  [i]the label you search with, like [code][color=#ffd36e]"pearl"[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]value[/color][/b]  —  [i]the data stored under that key, like [code][color=#ffd36e]3[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]use[/color][/b]  —  [i]brings a type from the standard library into your code[/i]

HashMap lives outside the default toolbox, so add this line at the top of your file:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]use[/color] std::collections::[color=#ffcb6b]HashMap[/color]; [/bgcolor][/code]

Making and reading one:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] shells: [color=#ffcb6b]HashMap[/color]<[color=#ffcb6b]String[/color], u32> = [color=#ffcb6b]HashMap[/color]::new();[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] shells.insert([color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"pearl"[/color]), [color=#f78c6c]3[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] shells.insert([color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]::from([color=#c3e88d]"conch"[/color]), [color=#f78c6c]1[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]match[/color] shells.get([color=#c3e88d]"pearl"[/color]) {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Some[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{n} pearls"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]None[/color] => [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"no pearls"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]insert[/color][/code] adds a pair (or replaces an old value with the same key). [code][color=#ffd36e]get[/color][/code] returns an [code][color=#ffd36e]Option<&u32>[/color][/code], because the key might not be there. That is the same safe idea as [code][color=#ffd36e]Vec::get[/color][/code].

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]get("pearl")[/color][/code] takes a [code][color=#ffd36e]&str[/color][/code], so you do not have to build a new String just to look something up.[/i][/color]

[b]Counting trick![/b] To count things you need "start at 0 if new, then add 1". The [code][color=#ffd36e]entry[/color][/code] method does exactly that:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] counts: [color=#ffcb6b]HashMap[/color]<[color=#ffcb6b]String[/color], u32> = [color=#ffcb6b]HashMap[/color]::new();[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] word [color=#c792ea]in[/color] [color=#c3e88d]"a b a"[/color].split_whitespace() {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] c = counts.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert([color=#f78c6c]0[/color]);[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     *c += [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// a: 2, b: 1[/color][/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]entry[/color][/b]  —  [i]asks "is this key already here?"[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]or_insert[/color][/b]  —  [i]if the key is missing, store this starting value; either way, hand back a mutable reference to the value[/i]

Because you get a reference, you write [code][color=#ffd36e]*c += 1[/color][/code] to change the number inside.

Looping over every pair:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] (name, count) [color=#c792ea]in[/color] &counts {   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{name}: {count}"[/color]); [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                [/bgcolor][/code]

Careful: a HashMap has [b]no fixed order[/b]. Run the program twice and the pairs may come out in different orders. If order matters, collect the keys into a Vec and sort them.

[code][color=#ffd36e]counts.len()[/color][/code] tells you how many keys there are.

Inside the loop: [code][color=#ffd36e]let c = counts.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert(0);[/color][/code] then [code][color=#ffd36e]*c += 1;[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]add_shells[/color][/code] uses the same two lines, but adds [code][color=#ffd36e]n[/color][/code] and uses [code][color=#ffd36e]who[/color][/code].

Something huge slides up from the deep, its tentacles stuffed with lists, text and labelled notebooks. To beat it you must sort the Kraken's [b]catch[/b].

Today's weapons:

   •  [b]Vec[/b] to hold lists ([code][color=#ffd36e]push[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]get[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e]for x in &v[/color][/code])

   •  [b]HashMap[/b] with [code][color=#ffd36e]entry().or_insert()[/color][/code] for counting

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Traits: a promise of skills[/color][/b][/font_size]

Crabs click. Octopuses blub. Different animals, but both can [b]speak[/b]. A trait lets you say "anything that can speak must have these methods", and then write code that works with every speaker.

[b][color=#e59cff]trait[/color][/b]  —  [i]a list of methods a type promises to have[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]impl Trait for Type[/color][/b]  —  [i]the block where a type keeps that promise[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]default method[/color][/b]  —  [i]a trait method that already has a body, so types may skip it[/i]

Here is a trait with one required method and one default method.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]trait[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Speak[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] sound(&[color=#c792ea]self[/color]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color];          [color=#7f8ca3]// required[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] shout(&[color=#c792ea]self[/color]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color] {         [color=#7f8ca3]// default[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]self[/color].sound().to_uppercase()[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]struct[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Cat[/color];[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]impl[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Speak[/color] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Cat[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] sound(&[color=#c792ea]self[/color]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c3e88d]"meow"[/color].to_string()[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]Cat[/color][/code] only wrote [code][color=#ffd36e]sound[/color][/code]. It got [code][color=#ffd36e]shout[/color][/code] for free, and [code][color=#ffd36e]Cat.shout()[/color][/code] gives [code][color=#ffd36e]"MEOW"[/color][/code]. A type may also write its own version of a default method to override it.

Now the payoff. A function can accept [b]any[/b] type that keeps the promise:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] announce(x: &[color=#c792ea]impl[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Speak[/color]) -> [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color] { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]format[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"Listen: {}"[/color], x.sound())    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                       [/bgcolor][/code]

Read [code][color=#ffd36e]&impl Speak[/color][/code] as "a borrowed something that implements Speak". Pass a [code][color=#ffd36e]Cat[/color][/code], a [code][color=#ffd36e]Dog[/color][/code], anything with the trait. One function, many types.

[b][color=#e59cff]impl Trait[/color][/b]  —  [i]in a parameter, "any type that has this trait"[/i]

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]&impl Speak[/color][/code] is the friendly way to write this. You will meet fancier spellings later, but they all mean the same idea.[/i][/color]

Some traits are so common that Rust writes them for you. Put [code][color=#ffd36e]#[lb]derive(...)[rb][/color][/code] above a struct:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] #[lb]derive([color=#ffcb6b]Debug[/color], [color=#ffcb6b]Clone[/color], [color=#ffcb6b]PartialEq[/color])[rb] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]struct[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Crab[/color] {                      [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     name: [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color],                  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                  [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]Debug[/color][/b]  —  [i]lets you print the value with [code][color=#ffd36e]{:?}[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]Clone[/color][/b]  —  [i]lets you make a copy with [code][color=#ffd36e].clone()[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]PartialEq[/color][/b]  —  [i]lets you compare two values with [code][color=#ffd36e]==[/color][/code][/i]

Without the derive, [code][color=#ffd36e]a == b[/color][/code] on your own struct will not compile.
lessons.goal: Fill in the Speak trait's default method, implement Speak for Crab and Octopus, write describe, and derive Debug, Clone and PartialEq on Crab.
hints: Start with the default method. Inside a trait you can call the other trait methods on [code][color=#ffd36e]self[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]self.name()[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]self.sound()[/color][/code]. Combine them with [code][color=#ffd36e]format![/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]speak[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]format!("{} says {}", self.name(), self.sound())[/color][/code]. For the impls, [code][color=#ffd36e]name[/color][/code] can return [code][color=#ffd36e]self.name.clone()[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]sound[/color][/code] returns a string like [code][color=#ffd36e]"click".to_string()[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]describe[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]format!("[lb]{}[rb]", x.speak())[/color][/code]. For the derive, write [code][color=#ffd36e]#[lb]derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)[rb][/color][/code] on the line right above [code][color=#ffd36e]struct Crab[/color][/code].

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Closures: functions in your pocket[/color][/b][/font_size]

A normal function needs a name and a spot outside [code][color=#ffd36e]main[/color][/code]. Sometimes you just want a tiny bit of behavior on the spot. That is a [b]closure[/b].

[b][color=#e59cff]closure[/color][/b]  —  [i]a small unnamed function you can store in a variable or hand to another function[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]capture[/color][/b]  —  [i]when a closure uses a variable from the code around it[/i]

The inputs go between two bars [code][color=#ffd36e]| |[/color][/code], then comes the body.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] add_one = |x| x + [color=#f78c6c]1[/color];         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] add = |a, b| a + b;          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], add_one([color=#f78c6c]4[/color])); [color=#7f8ca3]// 5[/color] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], add([color=#f78c6c]2[/color], [color=#f78c6c]3[/color]));  [color=#7f8ca3]// 5[/color] [/bgcolor][/code]

You call it just like a function. Rust usually works out the types by itself, so you can skip them. Compare with the long way: [code][color=#ffd36e]fn add_one(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 }[/color][/code].

Closures can [b]capture[/b] variables from where they were made. A plain [code][color=#ffd36e]fn[/color][/code] cannot do that.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] bonus = [color=#f78c6c]10[/color];                         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] with_bonus = |score| score + bonus; [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                         [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], with_bonus([color=#f78c6c]5[/color])); [color=#7f8ca3]// 15[/color]    [/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]bonus[/color][/code] was never passed in. The closure grabbed it from its surroundings. This is what makes closures so handy.

You can pass a closure to a function. The parameter type says "anything callable that takes an [code][color=#ffd36e]i32[/color][/code] and returns an [code][color=#ffd36e]i32[/color][/code]":

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] apply(f: [color=#c792ea]impl[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Fn[/color](i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     f(x)                                          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                                 [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]                                                   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] main() {                                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#82aaff]println[/color]!([color=#c3e88d]"{}"[/color], apply(|n| n * [color=#f78c6c]3[/color], [color=#f78c6c]5[/color])); [color=#7f8ca3]// 15[/color]    [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                                 [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]Fn(i32) -> i32[/color][/b]  —  [i]the shape of a callable: takes an i32, gives back an i32[/i]

[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Iterators: a conveyor belt of values[/color][/b][/font_size]

Instead of a [code][color=#ffd36e]for[/color][/code] loop with a counter and a pile of [code][color=#ffd36e]mut[/color][/code] variables, you can put your items on a conveyor belt and add machines along it. Each machine changes or removes items. At the end, something collects the result.

[b][color=#e59cff]iterator[/color][/b]  —  [i]something that hands out items one at a time[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]adapter[/color][/b]  —  [i]a belt machine like [code][color=#ffd36e]map[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]filter[/color][/code] that returns a new iterator[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]consumer[/color][/b]  —  [i]the end of the belt, like [code][color=#ffd36e]sum[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e]collect[/color][/code], that produces a final answer[/i]

Start the belt with [code][color=#ffd36e].iter()[/color][/code], add machines, finish with a consumer.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] nums = [color=#82aaff]vec[/color]![lb][color=#f78c6c]1[/color], [color=#f78c6c]2[/color], [color=#f78c6c]3[/color], [color=#f78c6c]4[/color], [color=#f78c6c]5[/color], [color=#f78c6c]6[/color][rb];[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] total: i32 = nums.iter().sum();            [color=#7f8ca3]// 21[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] how_many = nums.iter().count();            [color=#7f8ca3]// 6[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] doubled: [color=#ffcb6b]Vec[/color]<i32> = nums.iter().map(|x| x * [color=#f78c6c]2[/color]).collect();[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// [lb]2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12[rb][/color][/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]map[/color][/code] changes every item using a closure. [code][color=#ffd36e]collect[/color][/code] gathers the items into a new [code][color=#ffd36e]Vec[/color][/code]. Nothing happens until a consumer runs, because iterators are lazy.

[code][color=#ffd36e]filter[/color][/code] keeps only the items the closure says [code][color=#ffd36e]true[/color][/code] for. Add [code][color=#ffd36e].copied()[/color][/code] first so the closure sees plain numbers instead of references.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] big: [color=#ffcb6b]Vec[/color]<i32> = nums [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     .iter()              [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     .copied()            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     .filter(|x| *x > [color=#f78c6c]3[/color])  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     .map(|x| x * [color=#f78c6c]10[/color])     [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     .collect();          [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// [lb]40, 50, 60[rb][/color]          [/bgcolor][/code]

Chain as many machines as you like. Read it top to bottom like a recipe.

[b][color=#e59cff]filter[/color][/b]  —  [i]keep only items where the closure returns true[/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]enumerate[/color][/b]  —  [i]pairs each item with its index: [code][color=#ffd36e](0, "a"), (1, "b")[/color][/code][/i]

The same job both ways:

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// for loop[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] [color=#c792ea]mut[/color] total = [color=#f78c6c]0[/color];[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] n [color=#c792ea]in[/color] &nums {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]if[/color] n % [color=#f78c6c]2[/color] == [color=#f78c6c]0[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         total += n * n;[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#7f8ca3]// iterator chain[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]let[/color] total: i32 = nums.iter().copied().filter(|n| n % [color=#f78c6c]2[/color] == [color=#f78c6c]0[/color]).map(|n| n * n).sum();[/bgcolor][/code]

[code][color=#ffd36e]enumerate[/color][/code] is perfect when you need positions: [code][color=#ffd36e]names.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, s)| format!("{i}:{s}"))[/color][/code].

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: when a chain stops compiling, add a type like [code][color=#ffd36e]let x: Vec<i32> = ...[/color][/code] to see what the compiler expects.[/i][/color]

hints: Every answer starts with [code][color=#ffd36e]v.iter()[/color][/code] (or [code][color=#ffd36e]names.iter()[/color][/code]). Then add machines with dots, and end with a consumer like [code][color=#ffd36e].sum()[/color][/code], [code][color=#ffd36e].count()[/color][/code] or [code][color=#ffd36e].collect()[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]sum_of_squares[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e].map(|x| x * x).sum()[/color][/code]. For [code][color=#ffd36e]count_big[/color][/code], use [code][color=#ffd36e].copied().filter(|x| *x > 10).count()[/color][/code]. For [code][color=#ffd36e]evens_doubled[/color][/code], filter with [code][color=#ffd36e]x % 2 == 0[/color][/code], then map [code][color=#ffd36e]x * 2[/color][/code], then [code][color=#ffd36e].collect()[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]labelled[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]names.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, s)| format!("{}:{}", i, s)).collect()[/color][/code]. The [code][color=#ffd36e](i, s)[/color][/code] pattern unpacks the index and the name.
