[font_size=36][b][color=#7fd1ff]Errors you design yourself[/color][/b][/font_size]

[code][color=#ffd36e]Result<T, E>[/color][/code] says "I will give you a [code][color=#ffd36e]T[/color][/code], or an [code][color=#ffd36e]E[/color][/code] explaining what went wrong". Until now [code][color=#ffd36e]E[/color][/code] was a plain [code][color=#ffd36e]String[/color][/code]. Better: make an [b]enum[/b] with one variant per kind of problem.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] #[lb]derive([color=#ffcb6b]Debug[/color], [color=#ffcb6b]PartialEq[/color])[rb] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]enum[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color] {            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Empty[/color],                  [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]NotANumber[/color],             [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]TooBig[/color](u32),            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                           [/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]custom error[/color][/b]  —  [i]your own enum that lists the ways something can fail[/i]

A function that can fail returns [code][color=#ffd36e]Result<T, MyError>[/color][/code]. Return [code][color=#ffd36e]Ok(value)[/color][/code] for success and [code][color=#ffd36e]Err(MyError::...)[/color][/code] for failure.

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] half(n: u32) -> [color=#ffcb6b]Result[/color]<u32, [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]> { [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]if[/color] n > [color=#f78c6c]100[/color] {                            [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]return[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]Err[/color]([color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]TooBig[/color](n));   [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }                                       [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#ffcb6b]Ok[/color](n / [color=#f78c6c]2[/color])                               [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }                                           [/bgcolor][/code]

Callers can then [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] and handle each case. No crashes, no mystery.

Calling another function that returns [code][color=#ffd36e]Result[/color][/code] can get wordy. The [code][color=#ffd36e]?[/color][/code] operator does the boring part: on [code][color=#ffd36e]Ok(v)[/color][/code] it gives you [code][color=#ffd36e]v[/color][/code], on [code][color=#ffd36e]Err(e)[/color][/code] it [b]returns that error from your function right away[/b].

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] quarter(n: u32) -> [color=#ffcb6b]Result[/color]<u32, [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]> {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]let[/color] h = half(n)?;   [color=#7f8ca3]// Err? leave early. Ok? carry on.[/color][/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     half(h)[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]?[/color][/b]  —  [i]unwrap an Ok, or return the Err to the caller immediately[/i]

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: [code][color=#ffd36e]?[/color][/code] only works inside a function that itself returns a [code][color=#ffd36e]Result[/color][/code]. It is a shortcut for a [code][color=#ffd36e]match[/color][/code] with an early [code][color=#ffd36e]return[/color][/code].[/i][/color]

To print an error with [code][color=#ffd36e]{}[/color][/code], give it a friendly message by implementing [code][color=#ffd36e]Display[/color][/code].

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]use[/color] std::fmt;[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]impl[/color] fmt::[color=#ffcb6b]Display[/color] [color=#c792ea]for[/color] [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] fmt(&[color=#c792ea]self[/color], f: &[color=#c792ea]mut[/color] fmt::[color=#ffcb6b]Formatter[/color]) -> fmt::[color=#ffcb6b]Result[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         [color=#c792ea]match[/color] [color=#c792ea]self[/color] {[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]             [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]Empty[/color] => [color=#82aaff]write[/color]!(f, [color=#c3e88d]"nothing here"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]             [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]NotANumber[/color] => [color=#82aaff]write[/color]!(f, [color=#c3e88d]"not a number"[/color]),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]             [color=#ffcb6b]CrabError[/color]::[color=#ffcb6b]TooBig[/color](n) => [color=#82aaff]write[/color]!(f, [color=#c3e88d]"{} is too big"[/color], n),[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]         }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333]     }[/bgcolor]
[bgcolor=#1b2333] }[/bgcolor][/code]

[b][color=#e59cff]Display[/color][/b]  —  [i]the trait behind [code][color=#ffd36e]{}[/color][/code] printing, and behind [code][color=#ffd36e].to_string()[/color][/code][/i]

[b][color=#e59cff]write![/color][/b]  —  [i]like [code][color=#ffd36e]println![/color][/code], but writes into [code][color=#ffd36e]f[/color][/code] instead of the screen[/i]
lessons.goal: Finish the CrabError Display impl, write parse_shells (returns a Result), total_shells (use ?), and report (match on the result).
hints: Start with the Display messages: [code][color=#ffd36e]write!(f, "empty input")[/color][/code]. For TooBig, put the number in: [code][color=#ffd36e]write!(f, "{} is too big (max 100)", n)[/color][/code].

In [code][color=#ffd36e]parse_shells[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]let text = text.trim();[/color][/code], return [code][color=#ffd36e]Err(CrabError::Empty)[/color][/code] if [code][color=#ffd36e]text.is_empty()[/color][/code], then [code][color=#ffd36e]match text.parse::<u32>() { Ok(n) => n, Err(_) => return Err(CrabError::NotANumber) }[/color][/code], then check [code][color=#ffd36e]n > 100[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]total_shells[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]let x = parse_shells(a)?; let y = parse_shells(b)?; Ok(x + y)[/color][/code]. [code][color=#ffd36e]report[/color][/code] is a [code][color=#ffd36e]match total_shells(a, b)[/color][/code] with [code][color=#ffd36e]Ok(n) => format!("Total: {}", n)[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]Err(e) => format!("Error: {}", e)[/color][/code].

[code][bgcolor=#1b2333] [color=#c792ea]fn[/color] f(s: &str) -> [color=#ffcb6b]Result[/color]<i32, [color=#ffcb6b]String[/color]> {           [/bgcolor]

Everything you learned comes together here. You will build the battle system: a [code][color=#ffd36e]Hero[/color][/code] struct, a [code][color=#ffd36e]Describe[/color][/code] trait, a [code][color=#ffd36e]Move[/color][/code] enum, iterator chains to total up damage, and [code][color=#ffd36e]Result[/color][/code] with [code][color=#ffd36e]?[/color][/code] to read a battle script like [code][color=#ffd36e]"claw, pinch 4, retreat"[/color][/code].

Each passing test is one hit on the Leviathan.

[color=#ff8c7a][b](\/) Pinch:[/b] [i]Pinch tip: go one function at a time and run the check often. Every hit counts, and the compiler is your shield.[/i][/color]

hints: Take it one hit at a time. [code][color=#ffd36e]Hero::new[/color][/code] builds [code][color=#ffd36e]Hero { name: name.to_string(), hp: 30 }[/color][/code]. The default [code][color=#ffd36e]banner[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]format!("=== {} ===", self.title())[/color][/code].

[code][color=#ffd36e]damage[/color][/code] is a [code][color=#ffd36e]match m[/color][/code] with one arm per variant; [code][color=#ffd36e]Move::Pinch(n) => n * 2[/color][/code]. Then [code][color=#ffd36e]total_damage[/color][/code] is [code][color=#ffd36e]moves.iter().map(|m| damage(m)).sum()[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]count_big_hits[/color][/code] filters on [code][color=#ffd36e]damage(m) >= 10[/color][/code] then [code][color=#ffd36e].count()[/color][/code].

For [code][color=#ffd36e]parse_move[/color][/code]: [code][color=#ffd36e]text.trim()[/color][/code], compare with [code][color=#ffd36e]"claw"[/color][/code] and [code][color=#ffd36e]"retreat"[/color][/code], and use [code][color=#ffd36e]text.strip_prefix("pinch ")[/color][/code] plus [code][color=#ffd36e].parse::<u32>()[/color][/code] for the power. For [code][color=#ffd36e]parse_battle[/color][/code]: make a [code][color=#ffd36e]Vec[/color][/code], loop over [code][color=#ffd36e]script.split(',')[/color][/code], and write [code][color=#ffd36e]let m = parse_move(piece)?;[/color][/code] then push.

choices: parse_battle returns that Err right away
quizzes.explain: [code][color=#ffd36e]?[/color][/code] hands the Err straight back to the caller of parse_battle and skips the rest of the function.
quizzes.question: Inside parse_battle you write [code][color=#ffd36e]let m = parse_move(piece)?;[/color][/code]. If parse_move returns an Err, what happens?
